title: Bee-Bots & Everyday Tech
strapline: Press, predict, and watch it go where you told it.
intent: Programmable toys like Bee-Bots make cause and effect and early coding wonderfully concrete: you tell it, it does exactly that.
Sequencing a set of instructions and predicting the result is genuine computational thinking, dressed as play.
Planning a route is real positional and directional maths — forward, turn, how many steps.
Exploring how everyday technology works — buttons, cameras, torches, remote controls — builds understanding of the modern world children live in.
Debugging — 'it didn't go where I wanted, let's fix it' — is powerful, resilient problem-solving.
implementation: Start with free exploration of a Bee-Bot or floor robot before any 'task' — let children discover what each button does.
Model predicting and checking: 'I think two presses forward will reach the flower — let's see if I'm right.'
Make mats and routes linked to children's interests — a town, a story map, a treasure trail.
Introduce debugging naturally: 'It went too far — what could we change to fix it?'
Use rich positional and sequence language: forward, back, turn, first, next, then.
Include real everyday technology too — torches, cameras, remote controls, timers — and talk about how they work.
Keep it collaborative — children planning a route together, taking turns to add an instruction.
key_questions: Where do you want it to go — how will you tell it?
What do you think will happen when you press this?
It didn't get there — what could we change to fix it?
What comes first, and what comes next in your plan?
How does this everyday gadget work — what does it do?

impact.text: Children sequence instructions and predict what the robot will do, then check if they were right.
Children plan routes using directional and positional language — forward, back, turn, how many steps.
Children debug their instructions when the robot goes wrong, adjusting and trying again.
Children explore how everyday technology works and talk about what different gadgets do.
Children collaborate on a route, taking turns to add instructions and sharing their thinking.
Children reason and explain their plans, showing early logical thinking.

enhancements: Bee-Bots or simple floor robots, kept charged and available.
Mats and routes linked to current interests — a town, a story, a treasure trail.
Arrow cards for planning and recording a sequence of moves.
Real everyday tech to explore: torches, cameras, timers, remote-control toys.
Obstacles and targets to plan routes around and towards.
A challenge card: get the robot from the start to the treasure in the fewest moves.

playing_exploring: Children explore what the robot and gadgets do, discovering cause and effect for themselves.
They test their instructions and see the result straight away.
active_learning: Children stay with a route problem, retrying until the robot gets where they want it.
creating_thinking: Children plan a sequence, predict the outcome, and debug and adapt when it goes wrong.
